problem: It says the direct stress σ is the same in all three directions. For a thin spherical shell the membrane stress is equal in the two directions in the surface, while the radial stress is negligible and taken as zero. The text's own Hooke's law result ε=(σ/E)(1−ν) is for biaxial surface stress; if all three stresses were equal it would be ε=(σ/E)(1−2ν).
fix: Replace with: 'the direct stress σ is the same in every direction in the surface (two perpendicular directions); the radial stress is taken as zero. Hence ε=(σ/E)(1−ν).'

problem: The formula dV/V=(2σ/E)(1−2ν) is the volumetric strain (dilatation) of the wall material under biaxial plane stress, not the change in the internal gas volume. Since V is defined as πd³/6, the internal volume, this contradicts the standard thin-shell result and the worked example. Plane stress with zero radial stress is also already the standard assumption, not a stricter one.
fix: Delete the comparison, or label it clearly as the wall material's own volume change. For the vessel's internal volume use dV/V=3ε=3(σ/E)(1−ν).

problem: d was defined in mm in Section 1, but V=πd³/6 is labelled in m³. The unit of V follows the unit of d; the worked example uses d in metres. This unit inconsistency can cause conversion mistakes.
fix: State the unit convention explicitly: 'with d in metres, V is in m³; with d in mm, V is in mm³', or keep the units general.

where: Worked example step 3 and step 7; Quiz Q5 and Q6
problem: Expressions such as 75×10⁶/2×10¹¹ are ambiguous and, read strictly left to right, wrong; the denominator is meant to be (2×10¹¹). The numerical answers are correct, but the notation can mislead.
fix: Use brackets: 75×10⁶/(2×10¹¹), (150×10⁶)/(2×10¹¹), and the same in the quiz answers.

problem: 'A dished end is part of a sphere' is too broad. Ellipsoidal and torispherical heads, mentioned later, are not spherical over the whole profile. The membrane formula pd/(4t) applies to the spherical crown or a hemispherical head.
fix: Say 'A hemispherical end (or the spherical crown of a dished head) is part of a sphere...'
